candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate agrees with the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire's point to within about 200 meters and with Pleiades' representative point to within about 70 meters.

summary.text: Jericho, near the Jordan River in the eastern Judean lowlands, is one of the most anciently inhabited sites in the region; the Gospels set the healing of a blind man (or men) and Jesus' encounter with the tax collector Zacchaeus on the road through or near the city.

history.text: The Old Testament city associated with Joshua's conquest narrative is generally identified with the tell of Tell es-Sultan; by the first century AD the inhabited settlement had shifted about two kilometers south to a site built up by the Hasmonean and Herodian dynasties as a winter palace complex, which is the Jericho of the Gospel narratives.

scripture.textWEB: As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.
They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
As he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
He entered and was passing through Jericho.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.

otConnections.note: The account of Jericho's walls falling during Joshua's conquest is the Old Testament's best-known episode set at the site and is referenced in the New Testament at Hebrews 11:30.
